name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
description: Two labeled subsets of the 80 million tiny images dataset created to provide reliable class labels for object recognition experiments. The CIFAR-10 set has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes, and the CIFAR-100 set has 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
citeAs: Krizhevsky, Alex. Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. April 8, 2009.
rai:dataCollection: The labeled subsets were collected from the 80 million tiny images dataset. Students were paid to label a subset by filtering out mislabeled images from images retrieved using class search terms and their WordNet hyponyms. Labelers were assigned a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with hyponym search terms. Labelers rejected images not belonging to the assigned class according to specified criteria. The authors personally verified every submitted label, removed duplicate images using L2 norm comparison with a liberal rejection threshold, and split the data into training and test sets.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source was the 80 million tiny images dataset, which was assembled by colleagues at MIT and NYU by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. Images were downscaled to 32 x 32.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The 80 million tiny images dataset was collected over the span of six months; the paper is dated April 8, 2009. No explicit start and end dates are given for CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 labeling.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs and the like. The dataset was then divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly selected 5000 images from each CIFAR-10 class.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the underlying tiny images experiments, images were downscaled to 32 x 32. Perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed from the original tiny images collection. For modeling, data preprocessing included ZCA whitening, and in later experiments deleting the 1000 least-significant principal components by setting corresponding entries of the diagonal matrix D to zero. Some experiments also divided 32 x 32 images into 25 overlapping 8 x 8 patches plus a 26th 8 x 8 subsampled global patch.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. Because each image already had a noisy label from the search term used to find it, labelers filtered out mislabeled images. Each labeler was given a class and examined images found with that class as the search term and with hyponym search terms from WordNet. Labelers were instructed to reject images not belonging to the assigned class. Criteria included: the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?'; the image should be photo-realistic and not a line drawing; the image should contain only one prominent instance of the object; and the object could be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint if its identity was still clear. The instruction sheet also stated that false positives were worse than false negatives, multiple equally prominent objects should be rejected, cluttered backgrounds were acceptable, and duplicates need not be carefully rejected because they would be removed later. The authors personally verified every submitted label.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The dataset already came with noisy labels from search terms, and human labelers were used to filter out mislabeled images. The authors personally verified every label submitted by the labelers. Duplicate images were removed afterward using L2 norm comparison.
rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 1 human labeler review per item, plus personal verification by the authors; exact number not stated.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: WordNet was used to identify hyponyms for search terms; duplicate removal used L2 norm comparison.
rai:dataBiases: The original tiny images dataset labels derived from web search terms are described as extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. The images were collected by searching for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using web search engines and keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each term. The paper also notes that natural images in the dataset tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal, probably caused by the way people take photographs by making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object.
rai:dataLimitations: A problematic aspect of the tiny images dataset is that there are no reliable class labels, making it hard to use for object recognition experiments. The search-term labels are only rough labels and are extremely unreliable. Most experiments with unsupervised learning were performed on a subset of about 2 million images rather than the full 80 million. CIFAR-100 was only very recently completed, so all experiments in the paper used CIFAR-10.
rai:dataUseCases: The tiny images dataset is described as an excellent dataset for unsupervised training of deep generative models. CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 were created to provide reliable labels for object recognition experiments. In the paper, CIFAR-10 is used for training and testing classifiers, with 5000 randomly selected training images per class and the remainder used as test data. CIFAR-100 classes are mutually exclusive with CIFAR-10 classes and can be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10.
